You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

# task-a9b93d42: exterior background flood-fill

# task-a9b93d42: full monochromatic line recoloring (confirmed)

A solved instance showed that every complete monochromatic row and every complete monochromatic column is recolored to 2; all other cells are preserved. This applies to the color of the complete line, whatever that color is. At intersections, also recolor to 2. Preserve grid dimensions.

Confirmed solved test (14x24): input contained complete rows of 1 at 1-indexed rows 3, 7, 10 and complete columns of 1 at columns 3, 16, 18, 19, 22, 24. Correct output changed exactly those whole rows/columns to 2 (union of coordinates), preserving all cells outside them, including isolated 1s and 4 field marks. A directly constructed output matching this rule was accepted on a later attempt.

Demo evidence confirms line-color independence: demo 1 changed full 0 rows and full 0 columns to 2; demo 2 changed complete 1 rows/column; demo 3 changed complete 4 row/columns; demo 4 complete 0 lines; demo 5 complete 5 row/column; demo 6 complete 4 lines; demo 7 complete 3 lines; demo 8 complete 7 row/columns. In each, only the cells in complete single-color rows or columns became 2; unrelated matching-colored cells remained unchanged.

Implementation: collect all row indices whose cells are identical and all column indices whose cells are identical in the original grid, then recolor their union to 2. Use original input for detection; do not iteratively detect lines after recoloring. Verify dimensions/row lengths. This rule is more reliable than exterior flood fill: the first two test submissions based on exterior-connected background 4 were incorrect. An earlier manual line-based submission was also rejected, but the exact programmatically generated union of complete rows/columns was accepted; preserve cells outside the union exactly and avoid transcription mistakes.

Additional confirmed test: 20x10 grid using colors 6/8; complete rows (0-indexed) 3,4,5,8,10 and complete column 4 were detected and recolored to 2. # ARC grid output validation

Use alongside the ARC-solving workflow whenever producing a grid submission.

## Workflow
1. Record expected height and width from the task and demos; do not assume they match unless confirmed.
2. Construct the complete result from a structured grid representation rather than manually editing or truncating rows.
3. Validate exactly the expected number of rows, exactly the expected number of integer cells per row, and values restricted to 0–9.
4. Serialize as one valid JSON object with the required action key and complete grid. Check the actual emitted payload, not just the intended generator logic.
5. If feedback says the submission is not a valid ARC grid, first treat it as a shape/serialization failure: recount row lengths and inspect nesting for omissions, malformed rows, or extra payload. Do not blindly repeat the same representation.

## Pitfalls
- A conceptually valid output may still be rejected because JSON was malformed or a row has the wrong width.
- Large grids are prone to transcription errors; programmatic construction and explicit shape assertions reduce this risk.
